description: Triarchy, a hackathon team building fast, data-grounded, visually polished tools, from Godot games to AI agents to now, a NASA Space Apps mission trainer.
summary:
Team TRIARCHY developed Peaks of Eternal Light, an interactive game for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge’s Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Designed for kids ages 7–12, the game puts players in command of a lunar outpost near the Moon’s South Pole. They choose a landing site, place solar panels, grow food, extract water, and protect their crew from radiation while managing limited supplies.

Real NASA data shapes the lunar terrain and the Sun’s position, so a ridge can cast a shadow over a solar panel and reduce the power available to the base. At the end of each mission, a report helps players see how their choices affected the crew and what they could try differently next time.

The game gives kids a hands-on way to explore how science and engineering decisions affect life on the Moon. They can test ideas, learn from setbacks, and practice solving problems with limited resources.
details:
Team TRIARCHY built Peaks of Eternal Light for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge’s Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. It’s a 3D game for kids ages 7–12 that puts them in charge of a lunar outpost near the Moon’s South Pole. Their job is to keep the crew safe and supplied while deciding what to build, where to build it, and how to use limited resources.

Players choose a landing site, place solar panels, build greenhouses and water extractors, and explore the terrain in a rover. A hologram lets them preview and rotate a solar panel before placing it. They track power, oxygen, water, and food during the mission and decide when to spend resources on protections such as radiation shielding. At the end, a mission report helps players see how their choices played out and what they might try on their next run.

We built the game in Godot 4 using GDScript. We used elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to model the terrain. NASA/JPL Horizons data determines where the Sun appears at the simulated site and time, and NASA solar irradiance data informs the power estimates. These datasets create a gameplay consequence kids can see: when a ridge blocks the low Sun, a solar panel in its shadow generates less power.

Our creative approach was to turn lunar science into decisions players can make for themselves. A player might spend materials on shielding now or save them for a water extractor. We considered how much information a young player needs at each step, how to make changes in supplies easy to spot, and where to simplify the simulation so the choices are approachable. The intended impact is to give kids a place to test ideas, learn from setbacks, and practice the kind of problem-solving that goes into planning a space mission.
